title: games-market
summary: A test bench and catalogue of web games for live events: a projector is the screen and people's phones are the controllers. There are 18 registered, playable games out of 24 planned, in Canvas 2D, PixiJS and 3D, with deterministic physics and phone-to-projector networking without a game server.

facts.v: Test bench: not tried at a real event

tldr.v: Checking whether a game looks and plays right shouldn't require opening a real session or generating a room code. With 24 games planned, that doesn't scale.
A bench that opens any game instantly, with seed, simulated latency and loss, «Force end» and FPS in view. Whatever happens is shown and thrown away.
18 playable: 6 stable and 12 in beta, including the three 3D ones. The networked games haven't been tried on real phones yet.

p: A set of games for live events: a laptop with a projector is the screen, and each attendee joins with their phone through a QR code, with nothing to install. The repo is at once the bench where they are developed, the tool to show them and the catalogue.
list: Bench: opens any game, even a disabled one, with its settings editable live, seed, duration, simulated latency and loss, «Force end», the raw result and an FPS counter.
Kiosk: full screen with no sidebar and only the enabled games; when a match ends, it goes back to the grid by itself after 10 seconds.
Phone: it is the match's controller or runs the whole game on the phone, depending on what each game declares.
Games: from a snake game and a catapult to pool, a space game and a 3D shooter.

plan.h: The plan: order by technical cost
p: The 24 games were ordered into 12 batches by a score from 0 to 18: six axes (simulation, rendering, physics, network, content and input) from 0 to 3 each. The roadmap's rule: you can stop at any batch and the product still works. The three 3D games, the most expensive, were left for the end on purpose.

Today there are 18 playable: 12 in Canvas 2D, 2 in PixiJS, 1 in the DOM and 3 in 3D. Ten are enabled; everything multiplayer ships disabled and is switched on when used, though it can still be tried on the bench.
The other six were question and survey games for teams, and they don't exist as games in this repo. What is there is their shared engine (questions, grading, aggregation and ranking), with its tests.

net.h: The network: the projector in the middle
p: There is no game server. The projector simulates the match and is the only authority; each phone opens a direct channel to it, and phones don't talk to each other.

diagram.title: A star-shaped match
diagram.caption: Each phone sends its input and receives state snapshots, delta-encoded against the last tick it confirmed, with interpolation and prediction. Networked play needs HTTPS: a phone won't open WebRTC on an insecure origin.

host.label: Projector
host.note: It simulates the match and shows the QR with room, seat and seed. The protocol drops anything that doesn't come from the host: that is game consistency, not authentication.

p3.label: Phone 3
p3.note: Depending on the game, the phone is a controller or runs the whole match on the device.

broker.label: Signalling
broker.note: A public broker, only to connect: after that each phone talks directly to the projector over a DataChannel.

bc.label: Local mode
bc.note: During development, two tabs act as projector and phone over BroadcastChannel, with simulated latency and loss. The transport changes and no game notices.

p: Each game is an isolated module with three rules. That way the same game runs on the bench, in the kiosk or on its full-screen page without changing a line.
contract.title: From mount to finish

steps.d: Room, seed, duration, seat, who is host and how the network travels. The container decides, not the game.
It passes GameProps: that configuration, the settings with their defaults, the network and an abort signal. The game imports nothing from the shell.
A seeded PRNG and Rapier physics: the same seed replays the same match.
onFinish with {completed, points, durationMs, meta}. If the signal aborts, it hands over its partial result immediately.

contract.caption: The three rules are in the contract's header (src/core/contract/game.ts). On the bench, the result is shown raw and thrown away.

findings.h: What the first networked game found
p: The snapshot, interpolation and prediction layer was written early and went five batches without any game using it: its tests checked each piece on its own. The football game was the first to use all of it, and it found five problems: one was fixed with a regression test, two were documented and two are still open.

What did work, according to the repo's log: with 20 % simulated loss, 121 packets lost and zero decoding failures, because the delta is built against the last tick the receiver confirmed, not the last one sent.
The conclusion is written in the roadmap: a layer with green tests isn't tested until something really uses it.
There is no backend and no accounts, so what matters is not to promise what isn't there.

items.d: No accounts, ranking or saved scores: the result is shown and thrown away. The day a score is worth something, it gets validated on the server, never on the client.
The projector owns the state, but anyone with the room's QR can join. I don't claim anti-cheat.
WebRTC won't open on an insecure origin: Pages provides HTTPS, and locally there is a dev server with a certificate.
Private mode, a full quota or blocked site data throw errors, and the game still has to open.
The public signalling broker, to connect, and Google Fonts, for the typefaces.
CI runs lint and tests before the build and the deploy: publishing with a red suite is worse than not publishing.

items.why: A game receives GameProps, imports nothing from the shell, calls onFinish exactly once and, if aborted, hands over its partial result immediately.
A seeded PRNG and Rapier compiled to WASM: the same seed must give the same match, and that is what makes the netcode possible.
items.alt: Matter.js: easier to start with, but not deterministic.

items.why: WebRTC with PeerJS and the projector as host. The transport is swappable with BroadcastChannel; a TURN server only if needed.
items.alt: A game server of its own.

items.why: «A networked game that was only tested at 0 ms of latency is a game that wasn't tested»: the bench has adjustable latency and loss.

items.t: Each game in its own chunk
items.why: Rapier weighs 2.1 MB in 2D and 2.2 MB in 3D and can't be shrunk, so only whoever opens a game that uses it downloads it. Pixi and three are split out too.

«There are no render tests: they are expensive to maintain and don't catch the bugs that hurt in a game, which are about determinism and scoring.» The pure logic of each game, the engine and the network are tested.
items.alt: Render and e2e tests: they come in if the bench becomes critical.

p: TypeScript, ESLint and a CI that runs lint, tests and the build on every push to main before publishing. Each game's definition of «done» asks for 60 fps, zero allocations per frame, reduced motion and pause: it is a goal, not a measurement of every game.

items.d: 19 for games and 20 for engines, network, contract and UI
No e2e or render tests, on purpose

quality.note: I ran the unit tests with Vitest on 28/10/2026: 814 green, in 39 files. There are no e2e tests: that is a decision of the repo.

games.alt: The test bench catalogue: the title «Batería de experiencias», the counter «18 jugables · 6 pendientes» (18 playable, 6 pending), filters by category and topology, a sidebar with the games grouped by category, and cards showing each game's engine, topology and status (stable or beta).

status.h: Status and what I don't claim
list: Test bench: it hasn't been used at a real event.
18 playable out of 24 planned. The six question and survey games don't exist as games: their shared engine is what remains.
No networked game has been tried on real phones, and one shader hasn't been compiled on a real GPU yet.
60 fps is the goal in the definition of «done», not a measurement of every game.
No server, accounts, ranking or anti-cheat.
Two problems in the network layer are still open.
